questions.q: What does @zudojs/lifecycle manage, compared with @zudojs/runtime?
questions.explain: The ideas are the same (order, rollback, graceful shutdown), one level down. The lifecycle package also stands alone: it depends only on @zudojs/errors and @zudojs/constants.
options: Smaller parts called components (a pool, a queue worker, a server) with retries, timeouts, priorities and optional parts; the runtime manages modules

questions.q: Three components depend on each other: http → queue → database. In what order do the hooks run on start()?
questions.explain: A phase runs for every component before the next phase begins, and within a phase dependencies go first. When http becomes ready, every component has at least started.
options: database: initialize, start, ready; then queue: initialize, start, ready; then http
initialize for database, queue, http; then start for all three; then ready for all three
All hooks of all components at the same time
http first, because it was registered first

questions.q: Which work belongs in initialize rather than start?
questions.explain: initialize prepares; start connects; ready confirms. Keeping network work out of initialize means a configuration mistake fails before anything is opened.
options: Reading settings and creating objects, without touching the network

questions.q: What is manager.state after await manager.shutdown(), and can you call start() again?
questions.explain: disposed has no outgoing transitions. To run again, create and register a new manager.
options: disposed; no, a manager is used once

questions.q: According to LIFECYCLE_VALID_TRANSITIONS, where can a component go from failed?
questions.explain: A failed component is cleaned up, never "un-failed". Retrying happens inside a phase (the retry option), before the component is marked failed.
options: To ready, if the error is fixed

questions.q: cache and database do not depend on each other. How does the manager start them?
questions.explain: Independent components share a stage and run concurrently. Starting them one by one would add their times for nothing.
options: One after the other, in registration order
At the same time, up to the concurrency limit
Only one of them; the other waits for ready

questions.q: metrics has priority: 100; database and cache have the default. What does that mean?
questions.explain: Priority is a barrier: all components of a higher priority finish the phase before a lower priority begins. Shutdown is the mirror image, so the highest priority stops last.
options: metrics finishes each phase before the others begin it, and on shutdown it stops after them
metrics starts at the same time but is retried more often

questions.q: database takes 200 ms, queue (depends on database) takes 50 ms, cache takes 100 ms, all starting at 0 ms. When is queue up?
questions.explain: The queue waits only for the database (200 ms), then needs 50 ms. The cache runs alongside and does not delay it.

questions.q: When does the manager report a dependency cycle between orders and payments?
questions.explain: The whole graph is validated first. No connection is opened for an application whose wiring is impossible.
options: In start(), before any hook runs, as a LifecycleDependencyError naming the loop

questions.q: What happens if you call manager.register(...) after manager.start()?
questions.explain: Freezing the registry keeps the plan that is running consistent. Register everything before starting.
options: It is queued for the next start
It throws: the registry is frozen once start begins
It replaces a component with the same name

questions.q: A mailer registered with critical: false fails to start. What is the result?
questions.explain: Non-critical parts may fail without failing the application. Watch component:failed or the status so someone notices.
options: start() resolves, the manager is ready, and the mailer's status is failed
The mailer is removed from the manager

questions.q: The non-critical mailer failed to start. On shutdown, is its stop called?
questions.explain: The same is true for the component that fails during a rollback. Guard stop on the resource it closes.
options: No, only started components are stopped
Yes, in the published version, so stop must be safe for a component that never started

questions.q: A component always fails and is registered with retry: { attempts: 3, delay: 100 }. How many times is start called?
questions.explain: attempts counts retries. Plan the total time with that in mind.

questions.q: With retry: { attempts: 3, delay: 100 } and no backoff, what are the waits between calls?
questions.explain: Backoff is exponential unless you write backoff: "fixed". maxDelay caps a single wait (10 seconds by default).

questions.q: Which startup failure is worth retrying?
questions.explain: Retry transient failures: a service still booting, a timeout, a 503. A wrong password or a missing table fails the same way every time, and retrying only delays the message the operator needs.
options: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432 right after the database container started

questions.q: A component has timeout: 100 and its start takes 500 ms. When does manager.start() reject in the published version?
questions.explain: Waiting prevents a stop from running alongside a start that is still going. The cost is that a timeout does not free startup by itself.
options: At about 500 ms: the component is marked failed at 100 ms, but the manager waits for the hook to settle before rolling back
Never; the component succeeds at 500 ms

questions.q: A start hook returns a promise that never settles. It has timeout: 100. What happens?
questions.explain: Because the manager waits for timed-out hooks to settle, a hook that never settles hangs startup. Make the work itself cancellable, for example with AbortSignal.timeout.
options: start() keeps waiting forever in the published version

questions.q: What does passing AbortSignal.timeout(100) to a connect call achieve inside a start hook?
questions.explain: Cancellation has to happen where the waiting happens. The manager's timeout then acts only as a safety net.
options: The connect call itself gives up after 100 ms, so the hook settles and the manager can roll back on time
It aborts the whole process after 100 ms

questions.q: A component times out during start. What is the error chain of the rejection?
questions.explain: Each layer adds what it knows: the start failed, this component and phase failed, and why. Walk error.cause to reach the original.

questions.q: The HTTP server fails to start after the database and queue started. What does the rollback do?
questions.explain: Rollback leaves nothing open. To try again, build a new manager.
options: Leaves the database and queue running for the next attempt
Stops the started components in reverse order, disposes everything, and rejects start(); the manager ends disposed

questions.q: After a failed start you call manager.start() again. What happens?
questions.explain: start() and shutdown() are idempotent: they return the same promise every time. A retry of the whole start needs a new manager.
options: It returns the same rejected promise; nothing runs again

questions.q: During shutdown, the search component's stop throws. What happens to the others?
questions.explain: One broken part must not keep the others open. Because shutdown() still resolves, you must listen for the event to see the failure.
options: Shutdown aborts and the others stay open
They are stopped and disposed as usual; the failure is recorded in the results and emitted as component:failed, and shutdown() resolves

questions.q: shutdownTimeout: 200 expires while a worker's stop is still running. What happens?
questions.explain: Listening to context.signal lets the worker stop cleanly. The published version reports nothing when a hook is abandoned, so a shutdown that takes exactly the deadline is a warning sign.
options: Nothing; the manager waits for the worker
The manager aborts context.signal in the hooks' context and shutdown() returns; a hook that ignores the signal is abandoned without an error

questions.q: Kubernetes waits 30 seconds between SIGTERM and a hard kill. What is a sensible shutdownTimeout?
questions.explain: Your own deadline must fire first, so your clean-up (aborting work, closing connections) runs before the platform kills the process.
options: A few seconds below the grace period, for example 25 seconds

questions.q: What does the default handleSignals: true do?
questions.explain: Handlers are installed by start() and removed afterwards. The manager never calls process.exit() after a normal shutdown; the process ends when nothing is left open.
options: From start() until shutdown finishes, SIGINT and SIGTERM run shutdown(); a second signal exits with code 1

questions.q: A process has a @zudojs/runtime runtime with signal handling on, and a lifecycle manager inside one of its modules. What should the manager use?
questions.explain: One owner per process. Two handlers race, and the order between "stop the module" and "stop its components" is lost.
options: The default handleSignals: true, so both react

questions.q: In the shop example, why must the HTTP server stop before the queue, and the queue before the database?
questions.explain: Shutdown reverses the dependency chain: stop taking work, finish it, then release what it used. With the queue's dependsOn missing, orders stayed pending.
options: The server must stop accepting orders first; the queue then confirms what is pending, which needs the database still open
The database is the slowest to stop
It does not matter because dispose runs last

questions.explain: Components are critical by default. The failure rolls back what started (the database stops) before start() rejects, and the manager is disposed.

questions.explain: Two retries after the first call make three calls in total, and the third succeeds.

questions.explain: The 50 ms deadline aborts the signal long before the 2-second flush. The hook reacts, clears its timer and resolves, so nothing keeps the process alive.

questions.q: Write stages(components): group component names into stages so that every component comes in a later stage than all of its dependsOn, and each stage is as early as possible. Keep registration order inside a stage.
questions.explain: A component's stage is one more than its deepest dependency. Everything in one stage can run in parallel; shutdown walks the stages backwards.

questions.q: Write retryDelays({ attempts, delay, maxDelay, backoff }) returning the list of waits before each retry: delay every time for "fixed", doubling for "exponential" (the default), never above maxDelay (default 10000).
questions.explain: These are the waits the manager used in the lesson. Adding them up tells you how long a failing dependency can delay startup before the error appears.

questions.q: Write async withRetry(fn, attempts): call fn(); if it throws, retry up to attempts more times; return the first successful result, or throw the last error. (No waiting needed here.)
questions.explain: i <= attempts gives one first call plus attempts retries, the same counting as the lifecycle option. return await matters: without await, a rejected promise would escape the try.

questions.q: Write connect(ms, signal) that resolves "connected" after ms milliseconds, but rejects with signal.reason as soon as the signal aborts (and clears its timer). Then use AbortSignal.timeout(50) so the slow connection gives up.
questions.explain: The waiting code itself listens for cancellation, which is what makes a startup timeout effective. AbortSignal.timeout aborts with a DOMException named TimeoutError.

questions.q: Write walk(path) that checks a list of states against the transition table and returns "ok", or "FROM -> TO is not allowed" for the first illegal step.
questions.explain: The table is the whole state machine. A failed component can only be cleaned up; retrying happens before it is marked failed.
questions.expected:
ok
failed -> starting is not allowed

questions.q: Write async startAll(components): call each start() in order; if one throws, call stop() on the components that already started, in reverse order, then rethrow.
questions.explain: Only what started is stopped, in reverse. Unlike this version, the published manager also calls stop on the component that failed, which is why real stop hooks must tolerate that.
questions.expected:
start database
start queue
stop queue
stop database
http: EADDRINUSE

questions.q: Write async stopWithDeadline(stops, ms): run all stop functions at the same time, each receiving an AbortSignal; abort that signal after ms and return as soon as all stops finished or the deadline passed, whichever is first. Return "clean" or "deadline".
questions.explain: This is what shutdownTimeout does: race the stops against a timer and tell everyone to give up when time runs out. Clearing the timer on a clean finish keeps it from holding the process open.
questions.expected:
cache closed
clean
cache closed
worker aborted
deadline
